headline: Sheepscot Stripers Hold the Day Shift While Monhegan Mackerel Thin Out
subhead: Cool Gulf water keeps bass biting through the afternoon in the rivermouths, but the mackerel schools off Monhegan have gone quiet and the groundfish are sitting deep in the bay.
body_markdown:
My father used to say the Sheepscot never lies to you, it just don't always tell you what you want to hear. I was maybe fourteen, standing on the ledge below the old boatyard with a bucktail jig and no clue what I was doing, when he told me that. Forty-some years later I still go back to that same stretch of river most August mornings, and this week it told me the truth again: the bass are here, they're eating, and they don't care what time of day it is — which, if you fish south of us, sounds like a small miracle right about now.

That's the story of this week in Midcoast waters. While the water south of the Cape has stripers pinned to a strict dawn-and-dusk pattern because of the heat, our end of the Gulf of Maine stays cold enough that the fish never fully shut down. I've been working the mouth of the Sheepscot and up into the Back River on the last two hours of the incoming, throwing a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse tube trailer, and connecting with schoolie bass from 20 to 26 inches steady through the middle of the day. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but it's honest fishing, and there's enough of them stacked on the current seams below Barter's Island that a slow afternoon can still put a dozen fish in the boat.

The Damariscotta's been similar — bigger fish showing on the flood around Glidden Ledge, taking live mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet, right where the river narrows and the tide really starts to push. If you've got a livewell full of mackerel, that's the play up there right now, not lures.

On the subject of mackerel — that's where I've got to be straight with you. Monhegan used to be a lock this time of year, jigging Diamond jigs or mack trees off the east side around the mooring field and filling a five-gallon bucket in twenty minutes. This week the schools have thinned considerably. I made the run out from Boothbay Tuesday expecting the usual and came back with maybe fifteen fish after two hours of hunting. They're around, but scattered and moving, not holding in the tight balls we saw in July. My guess is the bait's dispersed with the bigger tides we've had the past several days — heavier current tends to spread mackerel schools out rather than let them bunch up tight against structure. If you're headed to Monhegan for mackerel this week, don't plan your whole trip around it. Have a Plan B.

That Plan B, for me, has been bass and bluefish working the tide rip off Eastern Egg Rock. The puffins are still feeding chicks out there, and where there's bait for the birds there's usually bait for stripers underneath. I picked up several bluefish in the 3-to-5-pound class working topwater poppers along the western edge of the rock on the last of the ebb, along with a handful of keeper bass mixed in. Nothing explosive, but a solid hour of fish on nearly every cast when the tide's really moving.

Further out in Penobscot Bay, the groundfish have done what they always do this time of year — they've gone deep and stayed there. I fished the channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven last weekend, working the deeper cuts in 90 to 120 feet with diamond jigs and cod rigs baited with clam, and found a mix of small cod and a few decent pollock holding tight to the bottom structure. The pollock action was better up on top than down deep, actually — around Saddleback Ledge and off the west side of Isle au Haut, we had pollock busting bait right on the surface in the early morning, chasing what looked like young herring. Casting a 2-ounce diamond jig or a Slug-Go into the boils there produced fast action for an hour before the sun got up and pushed them back down.

Haddock have been harder to come by close to shore — you're better off running out toward Matinicus if you want a real crack at them, working the deeper water in 150 feet or better. I haven't made that run myself this week, but a few of the boats out of Stonington have reported decent numbers on the drift with clam-baited rigs, which tracks with where they usually sit this time of year once inshore water starts to warm up in the shallower parts of the bay.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically through the coming week. The tides will ease back some as we move off this stretch of bigger water, which should let the mackerel schools tighten back up — if that happens, Monhegan and the ledges off Boothbay Harbor should turn back on within a few days. The rivermouth bass bite should hold steady as long as the Gulf stays cool, which it will. If I had one day to fish, I'd take the last two hours of an incoming tide on the Sheepscot or Damariscotta, work the current seams with bucktails or live mackerel, and not worry about the clock. That's been the most dependable thing going all week.
